description: We are End Space, a team of two developers from Pavlodar, Kazakhstan, passionate about technology, AI, and space exploration. We have experience in software development, hackathons, web applications, and performance optimization. Our goal is to build innovative, practical solutions using NASA data and modern technologies. We value teamwork, creativity, and strong technical execution.
summary:
MARSCOPE is a browser-based Marswalk planner for future astronauts on Mars. It layers data from several NASA missions over one site on Mount Sharp in Gale crater: HiRISE, CTX and Viking imagery, a 1 m HiRISE terrain model, MOLA elevation, THEMIS infrared, the USGS geologic map, and Curiosity's traverse, camera views, weather reports and radiation measurements.

On a 4 m terrain grid it plans a walking route from a habitat to science targets and back, staying within a 20° slope limit. It compares three routes (fastest, energy-efficient and cautious), estimates walking time, energy and background radiation dose, and checks from every point of the route that the crew can still return. The result is a clear mission status: GO, NO-GO, UNVERIFIED or NO ROUTE.

A surface EVA is only worth planning if the crew can get back. MARSCOPE shows that trade-off openly. Its limits are prototype planning assumptions, not validated NASA safety limits. Source code on GitHub — https://github.com/TimurK07/MARSCOPE
details:
WHAT IT DOES
MARSCOPE is a web application for planning a surface EVA ("Marswalk") on Mount Sharp in Gale crater. It opens on an interactive 3D globe of Mars, zooms into Gale crater, and continues into a 2D mission workspace over a study area of about 4.1 × 4.1 km. The user places a habitat and science targets; MARSCOPE plans the walking route out and back and reports a mission status: GO, NO-GO, UNVERIFIED or NO ROUTE.

HOW IT WORKS
From NASA's 1 m HiRISE terrain model we build a 4 m routing grid (1024 × 1024 cells) with elevation and slope. An A* search finds a route that never crosses ground steeper than 20°. For the same checkpoints it computes three routes: Fastest, Energy-efficient and Cautious, and compares them side by side. For every point of the route it searches for a way back to the habitat within both a distance and a time limit. Walking time and energy come from published models (Marquez 2007 and Santee et al. 2001, as used in NASA's SEXTANT planner); background radiation dose comes from the surface rate published from Curiosity's RAD instrument. Map layers add imagery, slope hazard, hidden steep ground, elevation contours, thermal infrared, geology, Curiosity's traverse with its camera views, and the latest weather report.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
NASA's Mars data is rich but spread across tools built for regional and global views. MARSCOPE brings it together at the scale of a single walk and turns it into a decision a crew could act on: can we reach this target and still get home? It shows the reason behind every verdict and what would fix a failing plan.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED
Honesty about limits. The 20° slope limit, 8-hour EVA, 2 km/h planning pace and return limits of 2 km and 60 minutes are our prototype assumptions, informed by NASA's Artemis lunar EVA concept. They are not NASA limits for Mars, and GO is not a safety clearance. When the return cannot be confirmed, the tool says UNVERIFIED instead of GO. We also considered accessibility (text contrast, keyboard use, touch targets) and phone use.

WHAT IS CREATIVE
One mission seen at three scales, from the planet down to a 4 m grid, without losing the plan. A "hidden steepness" layer that reveals steep 1 m ground inside cells that look walkable. Three routes shown as trade-offs rather than a single "best" answer.

TOOLS
TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet (2D map), three.js (3D globe), Web Workers; Python with NumPy and tifffile for terrain preparation; Vitest for 457 automated tests. No backend: everything runs in the browser.
